brain-computer-interfaces.today: Millions of people live with paralysis or have lost their speech after a stroke, spinal injury or ALS. Implants have let a small number of trial volunteers type, talk through a computer or move a cursor, but none is a standard treatment yet.
changes: Talk and type again at close to natural speed
Control a computer, wheelchair or robotic arm by thought
Live more independently, with less round-the-clock care

cancer-blood-test.today: Cancer kills about 10 million people a year. Most cancers have no screening test, so many are found only after they have spread, when they are much harder to treat.
changes: Catch cancers early, while treatment works best
Screen for many cancers with one blood draw
Fewer late diagnoses and fewer deaths

carbon-removal.today: Humans put about 40 billion tons of CO2 into the air each year. Even with deep cuts, climate targets assume billions of tons a year must also be pulled back out, and today's removal is a tiny fraction of that.
changes: Cancel emissions that are hard to cut, like from planes and cement
Bring CO2 levels back down over time
Limit warming and the damage it causes

cheap-desalination.today: About 4 billion people face severe water shortage for at least one month a year. Desalination works, but it uses a lot of energy, so it stays too expensive for many towns, farms and poorer regions.
changes: Reliable fresh water for coastal towns and cities
Water for farms in dry regions
Less strain on rivers and groundwater

clean-air.today: About 99% of people breathe air dirtier than WHO guidelines. Outdoor and household air pollution together are linked to about 6.7 million early deaths a year.
changes: Millions fewer early deaths from heart and lung disease
Fewer asthma attacks in children
Cleaner air often means less climate-warming pollution too

clean-water.today: About 2.2 billion people still lack safely managed drinking water. Dirty water spreads diarrhoea and other diseases that hit young children hardest.
changes: Far fewer deaths from waterborne disease
Hours saved every day carrying water, mostly by women and girls
Healthier children who stay in school

cure-hiv.today: About 40 million people live with HIV. Pills keep the virus in check, but they must be taken every day for life, and if they stop, the virus comes back.
changes: No more daily pills for life
No risk of the virus coming back
A one-time treatment that could reach everyone

cure-type-1-diabetes.today: More than 8 million people live with type 1 diabetes. To stay alive, they must check their blood sugar and take insulin every day.
changes: No more insulin injections or pumps
No constant blood sugar checks
Fewer complications in the eyes, kidneys and nerves

end-alzheimers.today: About 57 million people live with dementia, and Alzheimer's causes most of it. The newest drugs slow decline a little; none stops it.
changes: Keep memory and independence into old age
Spare families years of caregiving
Cut one of the biggest costs in health care

end-depression.today: About 280 million people live with depression. Many don't get better on the first treatments they try, and in poorer countries most people get no treatment at all.
changes: Treatment that works on the first try
Relief in days, not months
Care anyone can afford, anywhere

end-malaria.today: Malaria killed about 600,000 people in 2023, most of them children under five in Africa. Cases are rising again where funding has fallen.
changes: Hundreds of thousands of children's lives saved every year
Fewer sick days, more school and work
Money freed from nets and drugs for other needs

end-tuberculosis.today: TB killed about 1.25 million people in 2023, making it the deadliest single infection again. Treatment takes months, and drug-resistant strains are spreading.
changes: Over a million lives saved a year
No more months-long treatments
Drug-resistant TB stops spreading

feed-ten-billion.today: More than 700 million people went hungry in 2023, while farming already uses about half of the world's habitable land and drives most forest loss.
changes: Enough nutritious food for everyone
Farming that stops eating into forests
Harvests that hold up as the climate changes

fusion.today: Most of the world's energy still comes from fossil fuels. Fusion could give steady, low-carbon power from abundant fuel, but no machine has yet sent net electricity to a grid.
changes: Steady power, day and night, without CO2
Fuel from seawater and lithium, found almost everywhere
Little long-lived radioactive waste

grid-storage.today: Wind and solar are now among the cheapest ways to make electricity, but they rise and fall with the weather. Without cheap storage that lasts days or weeks, grids still lean on gas and coal.
changes: A grid that runs on wind and sun around the clock
Fewer blackouts and steadier prices
Fewer fossil plants kept running on standby

lab-grown-organs.today: More than 100,000 people are on the US transplant waiting list alone, and about 17 die each day waiting for an organ.
changes: No more waiting lists
No lifelong anti-rejection drugs
Organs made from the patient's own cells

mars.today: No human has travelled farther than the Moon. Mars is months away, with deadly radiation, thin air and no help nearby, so a crew would have to keep itself alive.
changes: A second home for people beyond Earth
Recycling of air, water and food that helps on Earth too
Science only people on the ground can do

moon-base.today: No one has been on the Moon since 1972. A base would need power through two-week nights, protection from radiation and dust, and regular supply flights.
changes: A permanent outpost for science and exploration
A place to practise living on Mars
Using Moon water and soil instead of shipping everything from Earth

restore-coral-reefs.today: Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but shelter about a quarter of all marine species. Since 2023, heat stress strong enough to bleach coral has hit about 84% of the world's reefs.
changes: Fish and food for hundreds of millions of people
Coasts shielded from waves and storms
Homes kept for a quarter of ocean life

restore-sight.today: About 43 million people are blind, and most of it could have been prevented or treated. For blindness from damaged retinas or optic nerves, there is often no cure.
changes: Read, recognise faces and get around alone
Work and live independently
Treat kinds of blindness that have no cure today

room-temperature-superconductors.today: Superconductors already run MRI scanners and fusion magnets, but they need deep cooling, which makes them costly and limits where they can be used.
changes: Power lines that lose no electricity as heat
Cheaper MRI scanners and stronger magnets
More efficient motors and electronics

slow-aging.today: Age is the biggest risk factor for heart disease, cancer and dementia. People live longer than ever, but many spend their last years in poor health.
changes: More years of good health, not just more years
Delay several diseases at once
Lower care costs as populations age

solid-state-batteries.today: Today's lithium-ion batteries use a flammable liquid and are close to their limits. Solid materials could store more energy more safely, but they are hard to make cheaply at scale.
changes: Electric cars that go further and charge faster
Batteries that don't catch fire
Lighter batteries for planes and devices

spinal-cord-repair.today: About 15 million people live with a spinal cord injury. There is still no treatment that repairs the damaged cord.
changes: Walk, stand or use your hands again
Regain bladder, bowel and sexual function
Less pain and fewer complications

useful-quantum-computing.today: Some problems in chemistry and materials are too hard for any ordinary computer. Today's quantum computers make too many errors to solve them yet.
changes: Design new drugs, catalysts and materials faster
Better batteries, fertilisers and solar cells
Today's encryption would have to be replaced
